practicalQuestion: How should carbohydrate, fluid, sodium, and recovery intake be organized across a same-day lift and field-practice schedule when the goal is to support both sessions without creating unnecessary gastrointestinal burden?

decisionContext.sport: Strength session followed later by field practice
decisionContext.outcome: Preserve training quality and between-session recovery
decisionContext.constraints: Four to six hours between sessions; campus dining options; variable sweat loss and gastrointestinal tolerance

evidenceConfidence.rationale: Only one source, a narrative review of young professional male rugby league players, gives between-session carbohydrate schedules for sessions less than 8 hr apart, and it cites earlier general guidance rather than testing it. The UEFA statement on elite football adds daily carbohydrate ranges, including about 6 to 8 g/kg/day for twice-daily training, and indirect gut-comfort guidance for match-day meals and in-match fueling. An observational study found higher body mass loss after the second of two practices on one day in heat, but those practices were about 12 hr apart, body mass loss stayed below 2%, and the authors judged that athletes were able to rehydrate between practices. No source tests a lift followed by field practice 4 to 6 hr later, and no source tests gut tolerance of between-session intake. Because there is not a second independent direct source and no source tests this decision, the tier is Limited.

dimensions.sourceReview: A narrative review of young professional male rugby league players, a UEFA expert group statement for elite football, a systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 small laboratory studies (half in endurance-trained males), an observational study of 31 male high school football players across 7 outdoor preseason practices, a smart-bottle validation study in 30 male American football players from one post-graduate team, and an observational dietary study of 185 Turkish collegiate American football players.
dimensions.directness: Low to partial. Between-session carbohydrate schedules for recovery of less than 8 hr appear only in the rugby league review, which cites earlier guidance and frames them for the preparatory phase when rapid glycogen restoration is the priority. Gut-comfort guidance is indirect (match-day meals, in-match fueling, carbohydrate type). The lift-then-field sequence with a 4 to 6 hr gap is not tested.
dimensions.consistency: Broadly consistent that heavy or twice-daily days need higher carbohydrate (about 6 to 8 g/kg/day), that recovery feeding starts early, and that fluid and sodium needs vary between athletes. The rugby league review also cites general guidance of 8 to 10 g/kg/day for 1 to 2 sessions daily while questioning whether 10 g/kg/day is realistic. The meta-analysis authors' suggestion that poor rehydration raises glycogen use is not supported by their pooled glycogen comparison.
dimensions.transferability: Mostly male professional rugby league and elite soccer players, laboratory studies in mostly endurance-trained or recreationally active males, and male high school, post-graduate or Turkish collegiate American football players. UEFA states its key recommendations are aimed at both male and female professional players, but no source reports between-session nutrition data in female collegiate athletes or in a campus dining setting.

bottomLine.text: No source tests a lift followed by field practice 4 to 6 hr later, so the evidence offers options rather than a tested plan. The rugby league review describes early carbohydrate and protein after exercise and, citing earlier guidance, two carbohydrate refeeding schedules for sessions less than 8 hr apart when rapid glycogen restoration is the priority. Expert sources say sweat rates and sweat sodium vary widely between players, so fluid and sodium plans should be individual. Gut tolerance between sessions is not tested; the available guidance is indirect, such as easily digestible pre-match meals and sports drinks or gels to limit gut problems during matches.

actions.title: Option: recovery feed after the lift
actions.text: The rugby league review states that about 80 to 180 g carbohydrate (1.0 to 1.5 g/kg) plus 20 to 67 g protein (0.25 to 0.55 g/kg) 0 to 2 hr after exercise will optimize glycogen resynthesis and muscle protein synthesis, while noting there may not be enough data for rugby-specific recommendations. It cites a small simulated rugby study (15 players) in which 1.0 g/kg carbohydrate at 1 hr after exercise very likely increased glycogen more than feeding at 2 hr, and notes conclusions are difficult from that sample. It also cites earlier work that about 20 g of high-quality protein soon after resistance exercise maximally stimulates muscle protein synthesis (40 g may be better for resistance-trained men), and states total daily protein should be prioritized over timing.

actions.title: Option: carbohydrate between sessions
actions.text: The rugby league review, citing earlier guidance, describes two schedules for the preparatory phase: 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg per hour for the first 4 hr when recovery between sessions is less than 8 hr, or an initial 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg within 1 hr after training plus 0.6 to 1.0 g/kg every 2 hr for 6 hr. It notes the amount needed depends on whether rapid restoration of muscle glycogen is the priority. With a 4 to 6 hr gap, the second schedule would run into practice. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): if rapid glycogen restoration is not the priority for a given day, or an athlete tolerates food poorly before practice, the lower-frequency option with smaller portions may be easier to manage.

actions.title: Option: limit gut burden before practice
actions.text: No source tests gut tolerance between a lift and practice; the guidance is indirect. UEFA advises that a pre-match meal be easily digestible to reduce the risk of gut problems and that comfort be considered, and notes that sports foods such as carbohydrate drinks and gels can minimise gut issues during matches. The rugby league review cites earlier work that after an early recovery feed, glucose plus fructose or sucrose appears better tolerated than glucose alone, and suggests feeding within 1 hr suits players who lack appetite right after exercise. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): applying these match-day and recovery principles to the pre-practice feed is a reasonable starting point.

actions.title: Option: fluid and sodium
actions.text: The rugby league review, citing the ACSM position statement, says athletes should avoid fluid losses above 2% of body mass during training. It states that during recovery, sodium in fluids at or above the concentration of sweat lost (20 to 80 mmol/L) is required to maintain positive fluid balance, which is somewhat higher than typical commercial sports drinks (about 20 to 25 mmol/L). UEFA reports that sweat rates (0.5 to 2.5 L/hour in male players) and sweat sodium vary substantially between players, and that players with both high sweat rates and high sweat sodium should get individual guidance. After matches, UEFA notes that in most situations normal eating and drinking can restore fluid and electrolyte balance.

actions.title: Option: make food easy to get between sessions
actions.text: The rugby league review suggests a nutrition table with appealing foods such as fruit, juice, cereal bars and milk drinks to encourage intake after training. UEFA notes that with the usual on-pitch session followed by resistance work and limited breaks, players cannot always eat whole foods, and lists sports foods as an alternative to meet nutrient targets. UEFA also notes, citing earlier work, that the order of gym and field sessions can influence habitual macronutrient intake, and in its recovery section advises meals and snacks providing 20 to 25 g high-quality protein every 3 to 4 hr. Turkish collegiate American football players in one dietary study ate low amounts of carbohydrate.

actions.title: Option: set the daily carbohydrate total by demand
actions.text: UEFA suggests 4 to 8 g/kg/day for preseason training and notes that twice-per-day training would likely require about 6 to 8 g/kg/day, with 4 to 6 g/kg/day where training is reduced or fat loss is a goal; in-season the suggested range is 3 to 8 g/kg/day. The rugby league review's own summary suggests about 6 to 8 g/kg/day. It also cites general guidance of 8 to 10 g/kg/day for intense training of 3 to 6 hr in 1 to 2 sessions daily, while questioning whether 10 g/kg/day is realistically achievable for heavier players.

monitoring.label: Body mass around each session
monitoring.text: Weigh before and after the lift and practice to track each athlete's fluid loss. In one American football study, fluid balance ranged from a 2.35% loss to a 0.47% gain across players. In high school players, body mass loss was highest after the second of two practices on the same day, though it stayed below a critical level. UEFA suggests self-assessing hydration each morning by body weight, thirst and urine colour when specialist support is not available.

monitoring.label: Do not rely on urine alone
monitoring.text: In high school football players, urine color and urine specific gravity did not significantly detect body mass loss of 2% or more, although the authors note their players did not reach that level of loss. Pair urine checks with body mass.

monitoring.label: Actual intake and gut symptoms
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): record what each athlete actually eats between sessions and any gut symptoms at practice, and adjust portion size, food type and timing. Session order can influence habitual intake, and match-day guidance emphasises easily digestible foods and comfort.

guardrails.text: These are population ranges from professional and elite sport, mostly male, not individual prescriptions. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): a sports dietitian should individualize targets, especially for athletes with medical conditions, body composition goals or eating concerns.

In high school players practicing in heat, urine color and body mass loss effects were greater after 2-a-day practices, though body mass loss stayed below a critical level. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): heat and hydration risk decisions stay with the sports medicine staff and institutional heat policy.
Do not apply one fixed fluid or sodium formula to the whole team, because sweat rates, sweat sodium and fluid balance vary widely between athletes.

limitations.text: No source studies a strength session followed by field practice 4 to 6 hr later. The between-session schedules come from a narrative review of young professional male rugby league players that cites earlier general guidance, frames them for the preparatory phase, and notes data may be insufficient for sport-specific recommendations. UEFA describes the usual order as on-pitch work followed by resistance work, the reverse of this question.

The hydration and glycogen evidence comes from 18 small laboratory studies, half in endurance-trained males. The pooled glycogen difference between rehydration and staying dehydrated was not significant and highly heterogeneous, and two included studies found glycogen resynthesis occurred even with poor or no fluid replacement.

The hydration carryover data come from 31 male high school players in hot preseason practices, with same-day practices about 12 hr apart rather than 4 to 6 hr. The sweat data come from one post-graduate team, and the collegiate dietary data describe intake only in Turkish players training 3 times per week, not performance.

whatCouldChange.text: Trials in collegiate team-sport athletes comparing between-session feeding schedules with a lift and a later field practice 4 to 6 hr apart, including gut symptoms and training quality outcomes.
Sweat rate and sweat sodium data from this athlete population, which would refine fluid and sodium targets.

evidenceTension.text: On daily carbohydrate, the sources largely agree on about 6 to 8 g/kg/day for twice-daily or heavy training; the rugby league review cites 8 to 10 g/kg/day general guidance for 1 to 2 sessions daily but questions whether 10 g/kg/day is realistic. On hydration and glycogen, the meta-analysis authors suggest poor rehydration may increase glycogen use in the next session, but their pooled comparison was not significant and highly heterogeneous, and two included studies found glycogen resynthesis was not prevented by poor fluid replacement. On fluid recovery, the high school study authors stress replenishing fluids between practices, while UEFA notes that after matches normal eating and drinking usually suffices.
